UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                      )
Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                            )                 Docket No. ER26-247-000
                                                      )


                           MOTION TO INTERVENE AND
                  SUPPORTING COMMENTS OF ITC GREAT PLAINS, LLC

        Pursuant to Rules 213 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“Commission’s”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 ITC Great Plains, LLC (“ITC Great Plains”)

submits these comments in support of Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP’s”) October 24, 2025

filing proposing revisions to the SPP Open Access Transmission Tariff to add the High Impact

Large Load (“HILL”) and High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”)

processes.

   I.         MOTION TO INTERVENE

        ITC Great Plains LLC is an independent, stand-alone transmission company engaged

exclusively in the development, ownership and operation of facilities for the transmission of

electric energy in interstate commerce. ITC Great Plains is a subsidiary of ITC Holdings Corp.

ITC Holdings Corp. invests exclusively in the electric power transmission grid to improve

electric reliability, facilitate access to low-cost generation, improve access to power markets,

stimulate economic growth, and reduce the overall cost of delivered electric power.

Transmission service over facilities developed and owned by ITC Great Plains is provided by




        1
            18 C.F.R. §385.213, .214 (2024).
                                                                         Docket No. ER26-247-000


SPP pursuant to its Open Access Transmission Tariff. ITC Great Plains is a Transmission

Owner member of SPP.

          As an SPP Transmission Owner, ITC Great Plains would be subject to the HILL and

HILLGA processes proposed herein. Thus, ITC Great Plains has a specific, direct, and

substantial interest in the outcome of this proceeding. ITC Great Plains has unique interests that

cannot be adequately represented by any other party. Accordingly, ITC Great Plains requests the

Commission grant this Motion for Leave to Intervene in this proceeding and permit it to become

a full party for all purposes.

    II.         COMMENTS

          As demonstrated in SPP’s filing, the proposed HILL and HILLGA processes are a just

and reasonable, forward-thinking effort to confront a significant and increasingly challenging

issue facing the SPP region. The massive, rapidly accelerating scope of large load

interconnections – in the form of data centers, crypto mining operations, electrified industrial

facilities, and other ultra-high demand users – is a phenomenon of which the Commission is

well-aware and which SPP has ably described in its filing.2 In concert with the United States

Department of Energy, the Commission is currently evaluating how to address this phenomenon

on a comprehensive basis through the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”)

issued in Docket No. RM26-4-000. This proceeding will no doubt benefit from commenter input

on these issues, as well as further advance Commission policy on large load interconnection.

Yet even as that proceeding develops, ITC Great Plains respectfully urges the Commission to

recognize that the HILL/HILLGA processes represent a reasonable, stakeholder-driven, and




          2
              SPP Transmittal at 6-11.

                                                -2-
                                                                              Docket No. ER26-247-000


commendably innovative approach to these challenges which the Commission should accept as

just and reasonable.

        a. SPP’s Proposal is Necessary to Maintain the Reliability of the SPP Transmission
           System

        Most importantly, SPP’s proposal is necessary and tailored to address the unique,

significant impacts that large loads have on the continued reliability of the SPP transmission

system. There is undoubtedly a glaring need for more streamlined and dedicated large load

interconnection processes, both at the SPP and national level; however, it is important to note

that SPP did not develop the HILL/HILLGA framework in a vacuum. These process

improvements were crafted by SPP while simultaneously developing large transmission

portfolios (2025/2026 Integrated Transmission Plan) driven by significant load growth, including

high impact spot loads such as HILLs. SPP’s proposed HILL/HILLGA process will attract new

large loads and facilitate their interconnection, while SPP’s regional backbone transmission

expansion plan will provide the system capacity needed to enable such load growth. Together,

these efforts will ensure reliable, affordable service to load and will bolster economic

development in the SPP region with the integration of data centers and manufacturing facilities.

Broadly speaking, traditional LSEs serve many small, geographically dispersed end-uses, such

that a single substation may feed dozens of MW spread over hundreds of feeders, whereas HILLs

concentrate hundreds or thousands of MW behind one interconnection point. For example, a 500

MW AI data center campus behind one 230 kV bus produces the same instantaneous load as

approximately 400,000 homes.3 This difference can produce significantly different impacts on

the SPP transmission system, which justifies a separate interconnection process.


        3
          Based on the average 10,500 kWh each American home consumes per year, which averages 1.2 kWh of
continuous load. United States Energy Information Administration, Electricity Use in Homes (Dec. 18, 2023)
(available at https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/use-of-energy/electricity-use-in-homes.php).

                                                   -3-
                                                                           Docket No. ER26-247-000


       HILL loads can impose high short-circuit duty at the interconnection bus, affecting

breaker ratings and protection coordination. Among other factors, this is driven by the use of

higher-capacity transformers with larger step-downs with low impedance, which can feed

substantial fault current during a system short-circuit event. HILL customers may also install

multiple parallel transformers for redundancy, each of which contributes additional fault current

to a short, thereby increasing the overall short-circuit duty feed substantial fault current during a

system short-circuit event. For large loads with co-located generation, these synchronous or

inverter-based generators near the load will add their own short-circuit contribution. Large loads

are also generally located physically very close to the SPP high-voltage system, resulting in very

low source impedance. These higher fault duties necessitate close coordination between

transmission owners and SPP to verify breaker interrupting ratings, relay settings, and bus

configuration limits. The HILL study process laudably provides an appropriate forum for these

analyses to be done in a timely manner.

       Large loads will also impact local voltage stability sensitivity, where disturbance at the

HILL’s node can have disproportionately large regional voltage/reactive effects. And as SPP

describes, HILL loads may also require electromagnetic transient (“EMT”) and voltage stability

studies that would never be justified for a single lower-sized distribution load. The proposed

EMT, Phasor Measurement Unit, forecasting tools, and ramp constraints provide SPP with tools

proportionate to risks that large loads pose to the reliability of the transmission system.

       As SPP notes, large loads generally draw power through rectifiers and variable-frequency

drives that exhibit little or no rotational inertia.4 For example, a data center’s uninterruptible

power supply and front-end rectifiers can ramp from near-zero to full load in < 100 ms.


       4
           SPP Transmittal at n. 48.

                                                 -4-
                                                                         Docket No. ER26-247-000


Conversely, a 100 MW electrolyzer array may shut down nearly instantaneously on frequency

excursions, injecting negative damping into local frequency response. In contrast to traditional

LSE loads which damp oscillations, these events can amplify forced oscillations and sub-

synchronous interactions among converter-based resources and adjacent synchronous machines.

SPP’s proposal ably addresses these considerations by requiring EMT studies where indicated, as

well as PMU installation requirements which will provide the high-speed telemetry which

standard SCADA systems cannot capture and which is necessary to identify and analyze these

types of issues after the fact.

        Large loads also exhibit significantly different ramp-rates and cycling behavior. Whereas

conventional retail and industrial load varies slowly with temperature and time of day, HILLs

can shift tens or hundreds of MWs in seconds due to process control or demand response

algorithms. AI training clusters may power up tens or hundreds of MWs of servers when a

compute batch starts, then drop that same load minutes later. Similarly, crypto mining facilities

ramp up or down rapidly as their profitability algorithms respond to price signals. These rapid

shifts and their attendant impact on the Area Control Error in the SPP region stress SPP in its

role as a Balancing Authority to provide regulation and frequency response service with

comparable ramp rates to comply with NERC BAL-series Standards. SPP’s proposed 20

MW/min default ramp-rate limit is an appropriate means to address these impacts in the near

term, although a higher limit would address the concerns more comprehensively. Similarly,

many large electronic facilities have internal protection logic that disconnects from the grid after

only a few voltage sags, in direct contravention of the ride-through requirements and

expectations for bulk-power assets. NERC has documented instances where large data centers




                                                -5-
                                                                          Docket No. ER26-247-000


tripped to backup generation after only a few voltage dips, exacerbating regional disturbances.5

A synchronized trip of multiple HILLs could similarly remove hundreds of MW of load within

seconds, causing overfrequency events. The significant threat of potential cascading instability

engendered by these operational characteristics of large loads is appropriately addressed by

SPP’s proposed HILL ride-through requirements, consistent with NERC Standard PRC-029

expectations.

       b. SPP’s Proposal is Narrowly Targeted to Address the Unique Characteristics of

             Large Loads in a Non-discriminatory Manner

       SPP’s proposal is also well-tailored to avoid any potential discrimination considerations

when compared to interconnection service provided to standard, lower-impact load and

generation customers. HILL/HILLGA eligible loads are materially different in character and

impact from traditional load-serving entities (“LSEs”). These differences are most prominently

reflected in the distinct, significant reliability challenges posed by large loads discussed in the

preceding section. Simply put, large loads constitute a different category of customer for whom

a different type of process is both necessary and appropriate.

       Beyond those operational and reliability differences, HILLs also proceed on different

timelines than traditional generation and load customers. As SPP observed,6 HILLs can request

interconnection on compressed timelines whereas legacy load growth was forecast years ahead.

Without a fast-track mechanism, SPP does not have the capacity within the existing Attachment

AQ/AX study processes to evaluate impacts or queue supporting generation before commercial

operation. In this context, the High Impact Load Delivery Point Study and optional HILLGA



       5
           SPP Transmittal at 20.
       6
           SPP Transmittal at 12.

                                                 -6-
                                                                         Docket No. ER26-247-000


path are properly viewed as reliability backstops rather than preferential treatment. On the latter

point, it should also be noted that HILLGA doesn’t give “extra” rights, as Load Limited

Resource Interconnection Service is both narrower and temporary (5 years), confined to local

service of the HILL, and expressly not NRIS/ERIS service, and insulates existing queue

customers. And the proposed higher fees/deposits/development milestones will deter speculation

and align with Order No. 2023’s commercial readiness provisions,7 ensuring that RTO resources

are not inappropriately devoted to serving HILL/HILLGA customers at the expense of traditional

LSEs and generators. And by assigning study and equipment costs directly to HILL customers,

the proposal preserves cost-causation principles and avoids undue cost shifts to traditional

transmission customers.

   III.        CONCLUSION

   Ensuring the reliable integration of large loads is both an economic and national-security

imperative. SPP’s proposal constitutes a well-considered and advanced approach to support

broader federal initiatives to promote U.S. leadership in AI, digital assets, and on-shored

manufacturing while protecting grid stability. The Commission will no doubt continue to

develop its large load interconnection policy in the existing ANOPR proceeding and elsewhere,

but in the interim, the Commission should accept SPP’s filing as just and reasonable, and

consider its features as the Commission seeks to establish best practices in the future.



                                Respectfully submitted,


                                              /s/ James W. Bixby
